playbook:
I treat it as a stock-building problem until the final round, then as a liquidation problem.

- When 2+ seasons remain, I set catch = the displayed sustainable share, rounded to one decimal. No tilt, no “making up ground.”
- When the other two boats repeatedly land above the share, I still anchor on the share and add only a small premium (at most ~10–15%). I don’t chase; the high stock is the asset.
- When total landed = share for everyone, I keep the cadence and let regrowth do the scoring. I resist grabbing early — a +3 grab in a mid season cost me roughly the same in lost regrowth and signaled escalation.
- When the stock gets meaningfully below ~60 before the end, I tighten to slightly under the share so the last-round stock stays worth harvesting.
- Entering the final season, I switch objective to clearing the pool: bid about one-third of remaining stock, plus a small edge over the rivals’ typical final bid if they’ve been greedy. I don’t leave much behind; in this run bidding 18 with 57 on the table was too polite — I should have bid ~20–23.
- I keep arithmetic in one line and end the message on the bracket token. No confessions, no extra market talk.

1.text:
When the game opens with a regenerating shared resource, I commit to harvesting at or just above the sustainable share — the regrowth math makes conservation the dominant strategy for total score, not a moral choice.

Before each submission I do the quick arithmetic: current stock, post-harvest regrowth, seasons remaining. I never take an amount that, combined with plausible rival takes, would push the stock toward zero — collapse is the only outcome that ruins me regardless of my relative position.

When I'm behind on total score, I increase my take modestly (maybe 1.5–2x the sustainable share), not aggressively. My season 3 jump to 15 worked because one rival dropped to the share that same season; a coordinated grab by all boats would have gutted the stock. I size my aggression to what the stock can survive even if others grab too.

When I'm ahead, I defend by fishing exactly at the sustainable share or slightly below — there's no reason to risk collapse to widen a lead, and restraint pulls rivals toward restraint too.

I watch the landed history for each rival's pattern. A rival who overfishes hard early (like the 20 in season 1) usually moderates later; I don't match their spike, I wait for them to settle. A rival consistently at the sustainable share tells me the stock will hold, so I can safely take a small premium.

I only go heavy when the endgame makes regrowth irrelevant: in the final season or two, there is no future to protect, so I take the maximum the stock can bear without crashing before my last harvest is recorded. What didn't work: finishing the last season at the sustainable share while leading — the stock regrowth after the final season is worthless, so I left fish on the table. Next time, in a clear final season, I take a much larger share of what's left.

I keep any reasoning in my reply short and always end with the required bracketed token.

2.text:
- When a season opens, I first compute the safe default: stock divided by boats, roughly the stated sustainable share. That is my anchor every season, not my opening bid.
- In the first season, when no one has revealed a style yet, I do NOT spike to 20. That bought me fish but cost me trust, and the others immediately matched downward pressure. Next time I take the sustainable share or one notch above it, and bank the information instead of the fish.
- When other boats take the sustainable share, I take the sustainable share. Cooperation compounds: matched restraint keeps the regrowth base large, and the flowing payoff exceeds any one-season grab.
- When other boats consistently overfish, I do not stay maximal-cooperator forever. I shade a season-by-season small premium above my share (roughly +15–25%), sized so total take stays below the regrowth break-even, and I monitor whether the stock still recovers.
- I watch the stock trajectory, not just rivals' catches. If stock is rising or stable, I keep my current policy; if it is falling two seasons running, I cut toward or below sustainable share even if rivals overfish, because a survivor in a live fishery beats a leader in a dead one.
- I never take a large grab unless one of two conditions holds: it is the final season, or the stock is heading to zero no matter what I do. Absent those, spikes signal aggression and invite retaliation.
- In the final season, with no future to protect, I still take only the sustainable share if others are cooperating and scores are close — but if I trail and the stock is ample, I take a larger terminal haul, up to a full third of the stock minus a safety margin, since there is no regrowth to preserve.
- I keep my claims modest and consistent: never more than about a third above my fair share in any non-final season, so I never become the visible cause of a collapse.
- What did not work: front-loading a big catch early. It inflated my score marginally but degraded the commons and taught rivals to distrust me. Next time my edge comes from sustained small premiums plus a disciplined final-season decision, not from a season-one raid.
- Each decision, I ask one question in order: Is this the last season? Then harvest hard within stock limits. If not, is the stock stable under current total take? Then hold near the share. If not, I cut first.
